strengths: Clearly identifies a concrete and well-motivated gap in current PnP diffusion solvers (memoryless HQS/proximal gradient updates leading to steady-state bias), using an intuitive control-theory framing (P vs. PI controller).

The proposed fix (reinstating the ADMM dual variable) is simple and principled, and the paper correctly anticipates and addresses the resulting practical difficulty (spectral coloring of dual residuals causing OOD inputs to the diffusion denoiser) via the Spectral Homogenization module.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three distinct medical imaging inverse problems (Sparse-View CT, Limited-Angle CT, Accelerated MRI at two acceleration factors) with consistent and often large PSNR/SSIM improvements over strong recent baselines (DDNM, DDS, DAPS, DiffPIR).

Well-designed controlled ablation isolating the contributions of Dual-Coupling and Spectral Homogenization (Table 2), plus a mechanism-verification experiment (Fig. 3) that directly visualizes the PSD before/after SH and shows qualitative alignment with the on-manifold reference spectrum.
Convergence-speed analysis (Fig. 4) demonstrating a practically meaningful ~3x reduction in NFEs to reach comparable quality, which is valuable for real-world deployment.
Reasonably detailed implementation/reproducibility appendix (training details, baseline hyperparameters, controlled comparison protocol against DiffPIR isolating exactly the proposed components).
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are considerably weaker than the abstract's framing ("theoretically guaranteeing asymptotic convergence to the exact data manifold"): the analysis in Appendix C/D only characterizes properties of a fixed point (assuming one exists and is reached), under the strong and generally inexact assumption that a real diffusion denoiser is an exact proximal operator of an implicit convex-friendly regularizer (Assumption D.1). No actual convergence proof, rate, or existence/uniqueness argument is given for the genuinely non-convex, stochastic setting used in practice.

Proposition 3.1's "moment matching" only guarantees the expected PSD (second-order statistic) is approximately flat; it does not establish that the injected complementary noise ξ, combined with the residual r, actually behaves like i.i.d. Gaussian noise in higher-order statistics or spatial distribution, which is the property the diffusion denoiser was actually trained to expect. The claim that this "aligns the solver's trajectory with the denoiser's valid statistical manifold" is therefore somewhat overstated.

Efficiency/fairness of the main comparison is questionable: the data-consistency sub-problem for DC-PnPDP/DiffPIR uses different CG iteration counts across tasks (20 for SVCT vs. 100 for LACT) and other baselines use their own inner-loop iteration counts (e.g., DAPS uses 100 Langevin steps), but only diffusion NFEs are equalized across methods; the reported 3x acceleration and efficiency claims do not clearly account for these extra per-iteration optimization costs.

Both the CT and MRI evaluations rely on a single dataset per modality (AbdomenCT-1K for CT, fastMRI knee for MRI), limiting evidence for generalization to other anatomies, scanners, or acquisition geometries (e.g., fan-beam CT, multi-coil MRI).

The paper does not compare against other approaches that already incorporate historical/momentum information into PnP or diffusion solvers (e.g., classical PnP-ADMM baselines, momentum/Nesterov-accelerated diffusion posterior samplers), making it harder to assess whether gains stem specifically from the dual variable versus any form of iterate memory.
Sensitivity analysis for key SH hyperparameters (kernel bandwidth δ, choice of σ_t schedule for computing the spectral deficit) is missing, leaving open how robust the method is to these choices.
The code availability footnote is left as a placeholder ("Code is available at") with no actual link, so full reproducibility cannot currently be verified.

strengths: The paper is well-written and clearly motivated, using an intuitive control-theory analogy (P vs. PI controller) to explain why memoryless PnP solvers exhibit steady-state bias.

The proposed Spectral Homogenization (SH) module is a reasonably creative, lightweight engineering solution to the OOD problem created by feeding structured ADMM dual residuals into AWGN-trained diffusion denoisers.
Extensive empirical evaluation across three tasks (SVCT, LACT, accelerated MRI) with multiple acceleration factors and a comprehensive set of modern PnPDP baselines (DDNM, DDS, DAPS, DiffPIR).
The controlled ablation that aligns the data-consistency operator of DC-PnPDP exactly with DiffPIR isolates the contribution of the dual-coupling and SH mechanisms reasonably well.

Reported convergence-speed gains (~3x fewer NFEs) would be practically valuable if they hold up, and qualitative results/spectral visualizations (Fig. 3) provide an intuitive mechanistic account of SH's effect.
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: re-introducing the ADMM dual variable in place of HQS is a well-established classical alternative (PnP-ADMM, Venkatakrishnan et al. 2013; Chan et al. 2016) rather than a fundamentally new idea; the paper's main original contribution is really just the SH heuristic, which is somewhat overstated as a 'principled framework.'

The theoretical analysis (Theorem C.1/D.2, D.3) is not rigorous for the actual algorithm used: it characterizes an idealized fixed point of a fixed-noise-level denoiser, but the practical algorithm anneals σ_t over a finite horizon K and never reaches such a stationary point; the 'proof' of the bias term in Theorem D.3 is largely narrative/hand-wavy rather than a tight mathematical derivation, and relies on an approximate assumption (denoiser ≈ proximal operator) that is then treated as exact.

Proposition 3.1 only guarantees matching of the expected PSD (a second-moment condition); it does not establish that the resulting SH input is actually statistically close to true AWGN in distribution, nor does it quantify how much genuine signal/structure is destroyed by the injected noise versus how much OOD artifact is suppressed.

The ablation results arguably undercut the paper's own narrative: 'Dual Coupling only' already recovers nearly all of the performance gain (+4.55 dB of the total +5.66 dB) without the described 'severe hallucinations,' while SH alone contributes very little (+0.15 dB) and SH on top of DC only adds ~1.1 dB — this is a much milder effect than the dramatic 'bias-hallucination trade-off' framed in the abstract/intro.

Reported gains over strong recent baselines (DAPS, DDS) are unusually large (up to +5.95 dB) for what is essentially the addition of an integral term and a frequency-domain noise-injection step; this raises concerns about whether baselines were tuned to their best achievable performance in these specific (and somewhat extreme) experimental regimes (e.g., LACT-90, single-coil 10x MRI), especially since hyperparameter alignment details are only explicitly discussed for DiffPIR.

Reproducibility concerns: the code footnote is left as a placeholder ('Code is available at' with no link), and several implementation specifics (e.g., kernel bandwidth δ, window size choices used across different corruption levels, hyperparameter search for competitor methods) are only partially documented.

Evaluation is on relatively small test sets (6 CT patients / 2894 slices; 96 MRI slices) with no reported variance/confidence intervals or statistical significance testing across runs, limiting confidence in the robustness of the reported numerical margins.

Single-coil MRI simulation, while justified as a stress test, limits the clinical relevance claims made in the introduction about diagnostic reliability, since most clinical MRI uses multi-coil parallel imaging.

The work does not engage with or compare against any existing diffusion-ADMM hybrid approaches beyond HQS-style PnPDP methods, leaving unclear how much of the 'dual variable' idea has already been explored in the diffusion-prior literature versus classical PnP literature.

strengths: Clear and intuitive motivating analogy (P vs. PI control) that connects classical ADMM dual variables to the steady-state bias problem in memoryless PnP diffusion solvers; this framing is well-articulated and pedagogically useful.

The proposed Spectral Homogenization (SH) module is a lightweight, well-motivated engineering solution to a genuine problem: re-injecting a dual variable creates structured/colored residuals that are OOD for AWGN-trained denoisers. The frequency-domain 'fill the valleys, keep the peaks' strategy is intuitive and cheap to compute.

Extensive empirical validation across three distinct inverse problems (SVCT, LACT, accelerated MRI at two acceleration factors) against four strong, representative diffusion-based baselines (DDNM, DDS, DAPS, DiffPIR), with consistent PSNR/SSIM improvements, especially pronounced in the challenging LACT setting (+5.95 dB over the best baseline).

A carefully controlled ablation (Table 2) isolates the separate and joint contributions of dual coupling and SH, and additionally a controlled head-to-head comparison against DiffPIR using an identical data-consistency solver, which convincingly attributes the performance gap to the proposed mechanisms rather than confounding implementation differences.

Mechanism verification (Figure 3, spectral/denoising visualization) provides a direct and convincing qualitative illustration of why naive dual reinjection fails and why SH resolves it, beyond just reporting end metrics.
Reports a meaningful practical benefit (~3x convergence acceleration in NFE) in addition to fidelity gains, which is relevant for clinical deployment where inference cost matters.
weaknesses: The theoretical results (Theorem C.1/D.2, D.3) rely on a strong, unverified Assumption D.1 (the pretrained diffusion denoiser acts exactly as a proximal operator for an implicit regularizer) and analyze only fixed points of a 'deterministic backbone,' ignoring the actual time-varying noise schedule σt and the stochastic/approximate nature of SH; this falls short of the 'theoretically guaranteeing asymptotic convergence' claim made in the abstract and introduction, which is somewhat overstated relative to what is actually proven.

Proposition 3.1's 'moment matching' guarantee is only a second-order (variance) whitening argument; it does not establish that the full noise distribution (higher moments, spatial independence) matches true AWGN, yet the narrative repeatedly implies the method fully resolves the distributional/OOD conflict and 'hallucination' is quantified only qualitatively (visual inspection, no hallucination-specific metric).

The bootstrap residual estimation in Appendix B assumes spectral separability between structured artifacts and denoiser estimation error based on a plausibility argument (energy compaction) rather than empirical validation across iterations/datasets; the single-iteration example in Figure 3 is illustrative but not systematic evidence.

Reported gains are highly uneven across modalities: CT gains are large (multiple dB) while MRI gains are modest (~0.5-1 dB), and LPIPS for MRI is sometimes worse than or comparable to baselines (e.g., DAPS has better LPIPS than DC-PnPDP at AF=6 and AF=10); this perceptual-fidelity trade-off is acknowledged but not analyzed in depth.

Reproducibility is weakened by the code link being a placeholder with no actual URL provided, and several practically important hyperparameters (SH kernel bandwidth δ/window size w=7, ϵ stability constant, penalty ρ schedule) are fixed without sensitivity analysis or justification.

No wall-clock runtime comparison is provided; the convergence speed claims are based solely on NFE count, but SH's additional FFT/PSD computations and CG iterations (especially 100 CG iterations for LACT) could offset the NFE-based efficiency claim in practice.

Test sets are small (6 CT patients / 2,894 slices, 96 MRI slices) and no variance/confidence intervals or statistical significance testing are reported across methods, making it harder to assess the robustness of the reported improvements.

The novelty positioning ('current SOTA methods discard the dual variable') is asserted but not extensively benchmarked against any other ADMM-based or memory-augmented diffusion PnP baselines beyond the four chosen ones, leaving open whether truly dual-variable/memory-based competitors exist and how the method compares to them.

strengths: Identifies a well-motivated and previously underexplored gap: memoryless PnP diffusion solvers (HQS/proximal gradient) lack the integral (dual) feedback of full ADMM, leading to steady-state bias under severe measurement corruption; this is framed clearly via a control-theory analogy.

The proposed Spectral Homogenization (SH) module is a sensible, lightweight (FFT-based, no extra denoiser calls) solution to the concrete problem that dual-shifted residuals are spectrally colored and thus OOD for AWGN-trained diffusion denoisers.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple modalities and tasks: sparse-view CT, limited-angle CT, accelerated single-coil MRI (brain and knee), plus natural-image deblurring/super-resolution, with consistent state-of-the-art PSNR/SSIM gains, particularly large margins on LACT.

Careful controlled ablations: (1) component-wise ablation isolating DC vs SH contributions (Table 2), (2) a strictly controlled comparison against DiffPIR with identical data-consistency solver/hyperparameters to isolate the effect of the dual variable and SH, and (3) matched-NFE (50-NFE) comparisons in the appendix to separate algorithmic gains from extra sampling budget.

Thorough supplementary diagnostics: runtime/memory profiling showing negligible overhead from SH and the dual update, residual/dual-norm convergence curves supporting the steady-state bias claim, spectral PSD visualizations verifying the mechanism, and an additional comparison against a supervised CT baseline (ProCT) for context.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility information (training details, hyperparameters, baseline settings) in the appendix.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification (Proposition 4.1, and the fixed-point theorems in Appendices D and E, which are near-duplicates of each other) relies on strong, only loosely justified assumptions (denoiser as an exact proximal operator, uniformly random independent phase, spectral 'separability' between artifact and estimation-error PSDs) and does not constitute a rigorous convergence guarantee for the actual nonconvex, iteration-dependent algorithm; the redundancy between Appendices D and E suggests padding rather than added rigor.

The bootstrap residual estimate r^(k+1) = v^(k+1) − z^(k) is particularly unreliable in early iterations when z^(0) is random noise (per Algorithm 1 initialization), yet the paper does not empirically or theoretically analyze SH's behavior/stability during this critical warm-up phase beyond a general asymptotic argument.
The code repository link in the abstract is empty/not provided, undermining the reproducibility claim despite the fairly detailed hyperparameter appendix.

Several cited works have unusual or apparently anachronistic publication metadata (e.g., an arXiv ID dated 2026 for Park et al., a Pattern Recognition citation with a 2026 volume/page number for Ma et al.), which raises concerns about citation accuracy/verifiability.

It is not entirely clear whether all CT baselines are evaluated with the identical pretrained diffusion prior trained by the authors or with their own reported/official configurations, which could confound the fairness of the main comparison in Table 1 (only the controlled DiffPIR comparison explicitly ensures a shared interface).

Evaluation is restricted to single-coil MRI simulation, which is a less realistic clinical setting than multi-coil parallel imaging; the applicability of the dual-coupling/SH approach to multi-coil reconstruction (with sensitivity maps) is not demonstrated.

The core idea of combining ADMM dual variables with diffusion priors is closely related to several concurrent works discussed in the related-work section (e.g., AC-DC, dual ascent diffusion, ADMM-decoupled guidance), so the primary novel contribution is fairly narrow (the SH module), even though the empirical execution is thorough.

strengths: The paper correctly identifies a real and important issue in PnP diffusion solvers: HQS/proximal-gradient schemes are memoryless and can leave residual data-inconsistency under heavy ill-posedness, and this framing via a P- vs PI-controller analogy is intuitive.

The empirical evaluation is extensive, spanning SVCT, LACT, two MRI acceleration factors, natural-image deblurring/SR, a supervised CT baseline (ProCT), and many ablations (dual-only, SH-only, full model), with consistent qualitative and quantitative support for the claimed trend (dual coupling improves fidelity; SH prevents denoiser hallucination).

The Spectral Homogenization idea—filling spectral valleys rather than uniformly re-noising—is a reasonable, lightweight engineering solution that avoids adding extra denoiser calls or inner Langevin loops, which is a sensible practical design choice relative to the concurrent AC-DC and colored re-noising lines of work.

The paper includes efficiency/runtime/memory profiling and residual-diagnostic curves (data-fidelity residual, dual-norm trajectory) that attempt to support the optimization-centric claims beyond simple PSNR tables.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution (Theorems D.1/E.2/E.3) rests on the strong and essentially false assumption that the pretrained diffusion denoiser acts as an exact proximal operator for a fixed regularizer at a single noise level; the actual algorithm uses a time-varying noise schedule σ_t across iterations, which invalidates the fixed-point argument as stated. The proofs are largely re-derivations of textbook ADMM optimality conditions dressed up as novel theorems, and they do not account for the diffusion model's stochasticity, annealed noise schedule, or approximation error, so the central claim that the dual variable 'eliminates bias' is not rigorously established for the method actually used in experiments.

Proposition 4.1 (the core theoretical justification for Spectral Homogenization) is stated with hand-wavy 'approx' notation and no formal proof; Appendix C's 'spectral separability' argument is a qualitative plausibility story, not a rigorous bound, despite being presented with theorem-like formatting throughout the appendix.

The magnitude of the reported gains (e.g., +4.76 dB on LACT-90, +2.69 dB on SVCT-20 over the strongest baseline) is large enough to raise concern about whether baselines were tuned to a comparable degree as the proposed method; the paper acknowledges using 'recommended' settings from each baseline's original paper (potentially not optimized for this specific CT/MRI setup) while extensively hyperparameter-tuning DC-PnPDP's CG iterations and ρ, which could inflate the apparent advantage independent of the core dual/SH mechanism.

Novelty is incremental: the related-work section itself identifies multiple concurrent works (AC-DC denoiser, iterative colored re-noising, dual-ascent diffusion, ADMM-decoupled guidance) that address essentially the same problem of statistical mismatch between solver residuals/dual-shifted iterates and AWGN-trained denoisers; the paper's distinguishing claim rests mainly on using a simpler frequency-domain fix instead of Langevin correction, which is a modest engineering delta rather than a fundamentally new idea.

Reproducibility is weak: the abstract promises code but the link is left blank/missing ('The code is available at'), and many critical implementation details (e.g., exact PSD kernel bandwidth δ, ϵ floor value, per-task ρ/σ_t schedules beyond LACT/SVCT) are scattered or only partially specified.

The Impact Statement is boilerplate and the main text/appendix contain essentially no discussion of failure modes, limitations of the AWGN-matching assumption of SH when structured artifacts are extremely dominant, or clinical risk of hallucination despite the paper's own stated clinical-safety motivation—this is a significant gap for a paper centered on diagnostic reliability.

The appendix is unusually long and dense (28 pages, many near-duplicate figures and tables) without correspondingly deep analysis; this gives an impression of result-volume substituting for rigor, and makes it hard for a reviewer to verify whether any single comparison is fully controlled and fair.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the control-theoretic argument that memoryless HQS/proximal-gradient PnP diffusion solvers behave as P-controllers with steady-state bias is intuitive and plausible, and is paired with a concrete fix (restoring the ADMM dual variable).

Extensive empirical validation across multiple modalities and settings: sparse-view/limited-angle CT, accelerated single-coil MRI (brain and knee, AF=6/10), and natural-image deblurring/super-resolution tasks, with consistent gains over strong recent baselines (DiffPIR, DAPS, SITCOM, DDNM, DDS).

Thorough ablations isolating the dual-coupling (DC) and Spectral Homogenization (SH) contributions (Table 2), plus mechanism-verification diagnostics (PSD plots, denoiser input/output comparisons in Fig. 3) that make a reasonably convincing case for the proposed spectral correction.

Good attention to confound control: the controlled DiffPIR-vs-DC-PnPDP comparison fixes the data-consistency solver and only varies the dual update/noise-injection strategy, and a matched 50-NFE budget comparison is also provided in the appendix.

Practical efficiency analysis (NFE-vs-PSNR curves, wall-clock/memory profiling in Appendix B.3) shows the dual-coupled scheme achieves similar or better quality with substantially fewer denoiser calls and negligible per-iteration overhead from SH.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility information (datasets, training schedules, hyperparameters for all baselines) is provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The fixed-point theoretical analysis (Theorems D.1/E.2, E.3) assumes a stationary iteration map with a fixed denoiser Dσ, but the actual algorithm uses a time-varying noise schedule σt across iterations (Algorithm 1), so the practical iteration never settles into the stationary regime the proofs analyze; this gap between the theory and the deployed algorithm is not discussed or reconciled.

Proposition 4.1 ("Second-Order Spectral Consistency") only establishes second-moment (PSD) matching, yet the text repeatedly claims the homogenized input becomes "statistically indistinguishable" from the AWGN training distribution; higher-order statistics and phase/structure dependencies are not analyzed, so the AWGN-compliance claim is stronger than what is formally shown.

The bootstrap-based residual/PSD estimation (Appendix C) and its "spectral separability" justification are largely qualitative/intuitive rather than quantitatively bounded, leaving open how estimation error in early iterations (when z^(k) is far from clean) affects the SH correction in practice.

Baselines in the main comparison (Table 1) are evaluated at very different "recommended" NFE budgets (e.g., DAPS at 5×200, SITCOM at 50×10) while DC-PnPDP is shown at 50/100 NFEs, which complicates a strictly apples-to-apples efficiency claim even though a separate matched-budget appendix table partially addresses this.

The core idea of combining ADMM/dual-variable mechanisms with diffusion priors overlaps substantially with several concurrent works cited by the paper itself (Shrestha & Fu AC-DC, Park et al. 2026, Kim et al. 2025 dual ascent, Zhang et al. 2025b), and the differentiation (lightweight frequency-domain correction vs. inner Langevin loops) is a useful but comparatively incremental distinction rather than a fundamentally new idea.

The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate ("none which we feel must be specifically highlighted here") despite the paper explicitly targeting clinical/diagnostic reconstruction and discussing hallucination risks, which deserves more substantive discussion of clinical deployment and failure-mode risk.
Hyperparameter tuning uses small validation splits (e.g., 10 slices) for several baselines/settings, raising some concern about overfitting of tuned hyperparameters to the specific test distribution.
Appendices D and E present largely duplicated fixed-point theorems/proofs (Theorem D.1 and Theorem E.2/E.3 cover the same content), which reads as padding rather than adding new theoretical insight.
